extraction.name: SciQ
extraction.description: A dataset of 13,679 multiple choice science exam questions created through crowdsourcing, with a multiple choice version and a direct answer version.
extraction.creator: Johannes Welbl, Nelson F. Liu, Matt Gardner
extraction.citeAs: Welbl, Johannes; Liu, Nelson F.; Gardner, Matt. Crowdsourcing Multiple Choice Science Questions. arXiv:1707.06209v1, 2017.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created with a two-step crowdsourcing process. First, crowd workers were shown three filtered textbook paragraphs from a science study-book corpus and asked to choose one paragraph or reject all three, then write a science question and correct answer based on the chosen passage. Second, another worker was shown the question-answer pair along with six model-suggested distractors, asked to validate whether the question could appear in a school science exam, and then select up to two suggested distractors and write at least one additional distractor to produce a total of three incorrect answer options.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: A small percentage of the passages were obtained from unreleasable texts, so the direct answer version of SciQ is slightly smaller, with 10481 questions in train, 887 in dev, and 884 in test.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The base corpus consisted of 28 science study books from online learning resources including CK-12 and OpenStax, covering biology, chemistry, earth science and physics from elementary to college introductory level. Individual paragraphs from these books were used as source passages for question generation. Existing 4th and 8th grade science exam questions were also used to train the distractor model.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A rule-based document filter was designed to classify sentences as relevant or irrelevant, and a paragraph was accepted if a minimum number of sentences was accepted. The final filter used lexical, grammatical, pragmatical and complexity-based rules to remove unsuitable sentences. The dataset was then randomly shuffled and split into training, validation and test portions, with 1000 questions each in validation and test and the remainder in train.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Individual paragraphs from the study-book corpus were filtered before annotation using a rule-based document filter. Sentences were filtered out if they were questions or exclamations, had no verb phrase, contained modal verbs, imperative phrases, demonstrative pronouns, personal pronouns other than third-person, began with a pronoun, contained first names, had less than 6 or more than 18 tokens or more than 2 commas, contained special characters other than punctuation, had more than three tokens beginning uppercase, mentioned a graph, table or web link, began with a discourse marker, contained absolute wording, or contained instructional vocabulary.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were produced by crowd workers in two stages. In the first stage, workers selected one of three candidate textbook paragraphs and authored a question and correct answer, following instructions such as no yes/no questions, no need for further context, querying general principles rather than highly specific facts, question length between 6-30 words, answer length up to 3 words, no ambiguity, and answer clear from the chosen paragraph. In the second stage, another worker validated the question-answer pair and created the multiple choice options by selecting up to two of six model-suggested distractors and writing at least one distractor themselves, for a total of three distractors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: In the first task, 12.1% of cases resulted in all three documents being rejected. In the second task, 92.8% of questions passed validation as suitable school science exam questions. Crowd workers included predicted distractors in the final question around half of the time, resulting in 36.1% of the distractors in the final dataset being generated by the model. A qualitative evaluation asked people to distinguish original science exam questions from crowdsourced questions; people identified the original exam question in 55% of cases, below significance under a random-guess null hypothesis.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Two human annotation stages per question: one worker generated the question-answer pair and another worker validated it and produced distractors.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers with Master's status; a total of 175 workers participated in the whole crowdsourcing project.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A random forest distractor prediction model implemented with scikit-learn; a rule-based document filter model.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper presents the dataset as a useful research resource for science question answering, including investigating neural model performance in medium-sized data settings and augmenting training data for answering real science exam questions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The authors note that conceiving original questions repeatedly can lead to specific lexical and structural patterns, and that their method was designed to enforce diversity in question content and lexical expression. They also note that some source types such as web search results yielded commercial or otherwise irrelevant documents, and Simple Wikipedia often stated highly specific knowledge.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The multiple choice version does not include the passage because the question is trivial to answer when given the correct passage, so systems must retrieve their own background knowledge. A small percentage of passages came from unreleasable texts, making the direct answer version smaller. The distractor model predictions were not high enough quality to use directly without additional filtering by crowd workers; some predicted distractors were semantically related but of the wrong type, misaligned in specificity, or unrelated or ungrammatical for multiword expressions.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training and evaluating science question answering systems. It has a multiple choice version, where the task is to select the correct answer using whatever background information a system can find given a question and answer options, and a direct answer version, where given a passage and a question a system must predict the answer span within the passage. The paper also uses SciQ as additional training data to improve performance on real 4th and 8th grade science exam questions.
